parole.significato: a suffix indicating the first-person singular preterite indicative of -ar
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese -ei, from Vulgar Latin *-āī, syncope of Latin -āvī. Cognate with Galician -ei, Spanish -é, and Italian and French -ai.

parole.significato: a suffix indicating the third-person singular indicative preterite of a verb in -ar
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese -ou, from Vulgar Latin *-āut, contracted form of Latin -āvit. Compare Galician -ou, Spanish -ó, and Italian -ò.

parole.significato: her, it (as a direct object; as an indirect object, see lhe; after prepositions, see ela)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese á, from Vulgar Latin *la (compare Spanish, Catalan, Italian, and French la), from Late Latin illa(m), feminine singular of ille (“the”, “that”).

parole.significato: to shake (cause (something) to move from side to side)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese abalar, from Vulgar Latin *advallāre, probably ultimately from Latin vallis (“vale, valley”).
From Vulgar Latin *evannāre or *advannāre, from *vannāre from Latin vannere.
From Vulgar Latin *abbracchicāre (later contracted to *abbraccāre in Proto-Romance), from Latin bracchium (“arm”).

parole.significato: to give someone something to drink
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese abeverar (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), from Vulgar Latin *abbiberāre. Cognate with Galician abeberar and Spanish abrevar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *abhorriō, from Latin abhorrēre.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese abraçar, from Vulgar Latin *adbracchiāre, from Latin ad- + bracchium + āre. By surface analysis, a- + braço (“arm”) + -ar.

From earlier abóbeda, from Old Galician-Portuguese boveda, possibly from the hypothetical Vulgar Latin word *volvita, alteration of Latin volūta, from volvere (“to turn”), but this presents serious phonetic difficulties. Compare Spanish and Galician bóveda. More likely of Germanic origin, from a Got
From Old Galician-Portuguese acabar, from Vulgar Latin *accapāre. Compare Spanish acabar, French achever and English achieve. By surface analysis, a- + cabo + -ar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese acatar, from Vulgar Latin *accattāre, from Late Latin cattāre, from Latin captāre. Compare Galician and Spanish acatar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese acolher, from Vulgar Latin *accolligere, from Latin ac- + colligere (“to gather”). Compare Galician acoller, Spanish acoger, French accueillir, Italian accogliere.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese acola (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), from Vulgar Latin *eccum illāc, from Latin eccum + illāc. Cognate with Galician acolá and Spanish acullá. cf. also Romanian acolo.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese acompanhar, from Vulgar Latin *accompāniāre. By surface analysis, a- + companha + -ar.

parole.significato: to happen; to occur; to take place
parole.testo: Derived from Vulgar Latin *contigīre, from Latin contingere. Compare Galician acontecer and Spanish acontecer.

parole.significato: to awake; to wake up (to stop sleeping)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese acordar, from Vulgar Latin *accordāre. Sense of "to wake up" was possibly influenced by Latin cordatus (“wise, prudent”), which would yield *cordado if inherited.
From Vulgar Latin *accursāre, from Latin cursus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum hāc.
From a- + delgaçar, from Vulgar Latin *dēlicātiāre, from Latin dēlicātus (“tender; delicate”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *addērēctiāre.
From Vulgar Latin *admonestāre, from Latin ad- + a cross of molestō (from molestus) and moneō (see admoneō). Compare Catalan amonestar, French admonester, Spanish amonestar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *addūbāre, from Frankish *dubban (“to beat”).
From a- + fio + -ar, perhaps from Vulgar Latin *affīlāre. Compare Spanish afilar, French affiler, Italian affilare. Doublet of afilar.

parole.significato: to drown (die or nearly die by staying underwater)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese afogar, from Vulgar Latin *affōcāre, alteration of Latin offōcāre. Doublet of ofegar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese [Term?], from a Vulgar Latin *affrontāre, from Latin ad frontem. By surface analysis, a- + fronte + -ar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese afondar, from Vulgar Latin *affundāre, derived from fundus (“bottom”). By surface analysis, a- + fundo + -ar. Compare Galician afondar, Spanish ahondar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese agosto, from Vulgar Latin agustus, from Latin Augustus. Doublet of augusto.
From Vulgar Latin *agurāre, from Latin augurāre. Influenced by the corresponding noun agouro. Doublet of augurar, which was borrowed from Latin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *acutia.
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Vulgar Latin *acūtiāre, from Latin acūtus, the past participle of acuō. Compare Catalan agusar, French aiguiser, Italian aguzzare, Occitan agusar, Spanish aguzar.

parole.significato: The name of the Latin script letter H/h.
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *aca, variant form of *acca (“aitch”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese al, from Vulgar Latin *ale, from Latin aliud, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élyos.
From Old Galician-Portuguese alegre, from Vulgar Latin *alecrem, from Latin alacer. Doublet of alegro.
From Old Galician-Portuguese algũu, from Vulgar Latin *alicūnus, from Latin aliquis + ūnus. Compare Spanish alguno, French aucun, Italian alcuno.

parole.significato: there (far from both the speaker and the interlocutor(s))
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ali, aly, from Vulgar Latin *adlic, from Latin ad (“to”) + illīc (“there”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese almorço, from Vulgar Latin *admordium, from Latin admordeō (“to bite or gnaw at or into”). Compare Galician almorzo and Spanish almuerzo.

parole.significato: alb (long white robe worn by priests and other ministers)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese alva, from Vulgar Latin *alba, from the feminine of Classical Latin albus (“white”). Doublet of alba. Cognate with Galician alba, French aube.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *albizāre. Senses 2 and 3 developed later. Derivable from alvo (“white; target”) + -ejar (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: a semicircular handle, such as the bail of a bucket and the handles of bags and purses
parole.testo: Deverbal from alçar (“to lift”), from Old Galician-Portuguese alçar, from Vulgar Latin *altiāre, derived from Latin altus (“high”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese alçar, from Vulgar Latin *altiāre, derived from Latin altus (“high”). Compare Galician and Spanish alzar

parole.significato: to dawn (to begin to brighten with daylight)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *admānēscere. Synchronically a- + manhã (“morning”) + -ecer (suffix forming verbs).
From Old Galician-Portuguese a mannãa (literally "at morning", in a similar sense to English tomorrow) from Vulgar Latin *māneāna. Displaced Old Galician-Portuguese cras.
From amargo + -oso, or less likely a Vulgar Latin root *amāricōsus, from Latin amārus. Compare Spanish amargoso, Sardinian marigosu, Dalmatian marcus.

From Old Galician-Portuguese [Term?], from Vulgar Latin *damascĭna-, for Latin damascēna (prūna) ("plums from Damascus"), whence English damson. Loss of initial d- probably due to metanalysis as the preposition de (dameixa → d'ameixa → de ameixa).

parole.significato: alder (any tree or shrub of the genus Alnus)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese *amẽeiro, from Vulgar Latin *amoenārium.
From Old Galician-Portuguese amizade, amiçade, amizidade, from Vulgar Latin *amīcitātem, derived from Latin amīcus (“friend”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese amolgar, from Vulgar Latin *admollicāre, from Latin mollis.
From Vulgar Latin *mōra, from Latin mōrum, from Ancient Greek μόρον (móron), from Proto-Indo-European *moro. Compare Galician amora, Italian and Spanish mora and French mûre.
From Vulgar Latin *amōrōsus, derived from Latin amōrem (“love”). By surface analysis, amor + -oso.
Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *admortīre, from Latin ad + mortem. Compare Spanish amortizar, Italian ammorzare, English amortize.
From Vulgar Latin *anteparāre (“to prevent”), from Latin ante- + parō. Compare Spanish amparar, Catalan emparar, Occitan aparar.

Many scholars have suggested ideas for possible origins, all of them lacking phonologically or semantically sound evidence to prove a certain origin. From Old Galician-Portuguese ameija, from which a Vulgar Latin *améiŭa, *ameiǫ́la can be reconstructed. Further origin unknown. Compare Galician ameix

parole.significato: almond (nut of tree of species Prunus amygdalus)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese amendoa, from Vulgar Latin *amandula, *amyndula, from Latin amygdala, from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē), of Pre-Greek origin. Doublet of amígdala and mandorla.
From Vulgar Latin *hanca, from Proto-Germanic *hankō (related to *ankijǭ (“joint, limb”)). Compare French hanche and English haunch.

parole.significato: rake (garden tool to sweep leaves and rocks)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *incīnus.

parole.significato: bird of the family Hirundinidae (swallows, martins and saw-wings)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese andorinna (“swallow”), from a Vulgar Latin root *harundīna, from Latin hirundō, hirundinem; cf. also harundō, which may have influenced it. Cognate with Galician andoriña, Mirandese andorina, Leonese andolina and Asturian andarina.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese anzolo, from Vulgar Latin *hamiceolus, diminutive of Latin hamus. Compare Galician anzol and Spanish anzuelo.

parole.significato: to put out; to extinguish (to stop something from burning)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese, from a Vulgar Latin *appācāre, from Latin ad- + pācāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *appascentāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *appicāre, from Latin picāre (“smear with pitch”), from pix (“pitch”).
From Vulgar Latin *ad poenam, with an additional adverbial /-s/ (compare entrementes, ultimately from Latin interim).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *appetēscere, from Latin appetere.

parole.significato: to second (to agree as a second person)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *appodiāre. Unlikely to be inherited. Compare French appuyer, Italian appoggiare and Spanish apoyar.

parole.significato: that (far from the speaker and listener)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese aquele, from Vulgar Latin *eccum ille, from Latin eccum + ille. Cognate with Spanish aquel.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese aqueste (“this”), from Vulgar Latin *eccum iste, from Latin eccum with iste.
From Old Galician-Portuguese aqui, from Vulgar Latin *eccum hīc, etymologically Latin eccum (“here he is!”) + hīc (“here”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese, from Vulgar Latin *aramen, variant of Late Latin aerāmen (“copper, bronze”), from Latin aes. Compare Galician arame, Spanish alambre.

parole.significato: to pant (to breathe quickly or in a labored manner)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *ār(e)fāre, from Latin ārefacere. Cognate with Galician alfar.
Unknown. The word implies a Vulgar Latin *arganāx. Possibly related to Galician argana, árgoma and argueiro, which would make it a word of Paleo-Hispanic origin.
From Vulgar Latin *arradicāre (compare Galician and Spanish arraigar), from Latin radicāre, from rādīcō (“to take root”). Doublet of radicar.

parole.significato: to harness (to place a harness on something)
parole.testo: Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *arredāre (“arrange, provide”), from Gothic *𐍂𐌴𐌸𐍃 (*rēþs, “advice”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese recadar, from Vulgar Latin *recapitāre. By surface analysis, a- + recader.
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Vulgar Latin *ad retrāre, from Latin ad + retrō.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese arreitar (13th century), from Vulgar Latin *arrēctāre (compare Neapolitan arrezzà/arrizzà), from Latin rēctus (“straight”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *remissāre, from Latin remissus, perfect passive participle of remittō, remittere.

parole.significato: to sequester the assets of a debtor, in order to ensure that they pay the debt
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Vulgar Latin *arrestāre, from Latin ad- (“to”) + restō (“to stop, remain behind, stay back”), from re- (“back”) + stō (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“stand”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese artelho, from Vulgar Latin *articlus, a syncopated/contracted form of Latin articulus (digiti). Compare the borrowed doublets artigo and artículo. Compare Galician artello, Spanish artejo, Catalan artell, Occitan artelh, French orteil.

There are at least two hypotheses: * Inherited from a deverbal formation derived from Vulgar Latin *ōsicāre (“to loathe”), from Latin ōdī (“to hate”). Compare Old Spanish usco (“disgust”). * Inherited from Latin eschăra (“scab, scar”), from Ancient Greek ἐσχάρα (eskhára, “hearth, brazier, scab”), co
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese aginna, from Vulgar Latin agīna, from Latin agō.

parole.significato: crux decussata (an X-shaped cross, used to crucify people)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *haspa.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *escharōsus, from Late Latin eschara, from Ancient Greek ἐσχάρα (eskhára, “scab left from a burn”). Indirectly related to English scar.
From Vulgar Latin *assedāre (cf. also *assediāre), from Latin assideō. Compare Spanish asear.
From Old Galician-Portuguese assegurar, from Vulgar Latin *assēcūrare, from Latin sēcūrus (“safe”).
From Vulgar Latin *(as)similiāre, a verb based on Latin similis (“similar”). By surface analysis, a- + semelhar. Compare Spanish asemejar. Doublet of assimilar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese assentar, asentar, from Vulgar Latin *adsedentāre, from Latin ad + sedentāre, or constructed in Old Portuguese as a- + sentar (“to sit”).

parole.significato: to point at, or in the direction of
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *sessitāre, from Latin sessum.
From Vulgar Latin *attītiāre, derived from Latin tītiō (“firebrand”). Compare Galician and Spanish atizar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese atras (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), from Vulgar Latin *ad trans, from Latin trāns (“beyond”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese aventura, from Vulgar Latin *adventūra, from Late Latin adventūrus, from Latin advenīre, adventum (“to arrive”), which in the Romance languages took the sense of "to happen, befall" (see also advir).

a- + vezo + -ar. Possibly corresponds to a Vulgar Latin *advitiāre (“accustom, habituate, familiarize”), from Latin vitium. Compare Italian avvezzare, Spanish vezar, avezar, Occitan avezar, envezar, Catalan avesar, cf. also Romanian învăța.
From Vulgar Latin *vīlitāre.
From Old Galician-Portuguese avoo, from Vulgar Latin *av(i)olum, ultimately from Latin avus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwh₂os (“grandfather”). Cognate with Spanish abuelo.
From Vulgar Latin *acerārius, from Latin acer.

parole.significato: holly (any of various shrubs or small trees of the genus Ilex)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese *azevinno, diminutive of *azevo (Compare Spanish acebo, Galician acivro, acevo), from Vulgar Latin *acifolium, from Latin aquifolium.
From Old Galician-Portuguese azinna, anzinna, enzinna, from Vulgar Latin ilicīna, derived from Latin ilex (“holm oak”).

parole.significato: holm oak (Quercus ilex, a tree of the Mediterranean)
parole.testo: From azinha + -eira. From Old Galician-Portuguese azỹeira, from azinna, anzinna, enzinna, from Vulgar Latin ilicīna, from Latin ilex (“holm oak”).
From the hypothesized Vulgar Latin *baba, ultimately imitative of children speech on the pattern of the repeated syllable ba. Compare French bave.
From Vulgar Latin *baccinum, from Gaulish.

From Old Galician-Portuguese badalo (“bell-clapper”), from Vulgar Latin *batāclum, from contraction of *ba(t)tuāculum, from Latin battuere (“to beat, to clap”). Cognate with Galician badal, Spanish badajo, Catalan batall, French batail, Italian batacchio.

parole.significato: to lower (to move something to a lower position)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bassiāre. By surface analysis, baixo + -ar.

parole.significato: to bathe; to give a bath; to clean by using water
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese bannar, from Vulgar Latin *baneāre, from Late Latin balneāre, from Latin balneum. Compare Spanish and Galician bañar, French baigner, Italian bagnare.
From Old Galician-Portuguese banho, from Vulgar Latin *baneum, from Latin balneum, from Ancient Greek βαλανεῖον (balaneîon).
From Vulgar Latin *barbūtus (“bearded”). Compare Spanish barbudo. By surface analysis, barba (“beard”) + -udo.
From Vulgar Latin *barra, possibly from Gaulish *barros (“the bushy end”), cognate with French barre and English bar. Doublet of bar.

From Vulgar Latin *barrum (“clay, mud”), from Paleo-Hispanic, possibly Celtic; compare Middle Irish broch (“waste, dregs”) and Gaulish *barros (“the bushy end”). Cognate with Galician, Mirandese, and Spanish barro, Asturian barru.
From Old Galician-Portuguese varron, from a Vulgar Latin *verrōne(m), from Latin verrēs.
From Vulgar Latin *bastāre (“to suffice”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese baço, from Vulgar Latin *hepatium, from Ancient Greek ἡπάτιον (hēpátion), from ἧπαρ (hêpar, “liver”). Compare Spanish bazo. Related to hepático.
From Old Galician-Portuguese beijo, from Vulgar Latin *baisu(m), from Latin bāsium, from Proto-Indo-European *bu.

parole.significato: to pinch (to squeeze a small amount of skin)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *vellicicāre, from vellicāre, most likely ultimately from vellus, the wool shorn from a sheep, fleece, or pelt.

parole.significato: welcome (whose arrival is a cause of joy)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese bem vindo, from Vulgar Latin *bene venītus, presumably a calque of a Frankish term, derived from Proto-Germanic *wiljakwemô (“a welcome guest or arrival”), from which many modern Germanic forms descend, such as English welcome. By surface analysis, bem (“well”)

parole.significato: to yell loudly or angrily, to scream
parole.testo: Either imitative or inherited from Vulgar Latin *verrāre, from verrēs (“boar”). Compare Spanish berrear and Romanian zbiera.

From Old Galician-Portuguese verça (likely via Galician verza or a northern pronunciation), from Vulgar Latin *virdia, from Latin viridia, neuter plural of viridis. Compare Spanish berza, Italian verza, Romanian varză.

From Vulgar Latin bīstia, variant of Latin bēstia. Doublet of besta. Sense of "homosexual" possibly influenced by the sense of "prostitute" or by English bitch (also related to the possible origin in Portuguese).
From Vulgar Latin *bīstius, a masculine form of bīstia, from Latin bēstia (“beast”). Doublet of besta.

From Vulgar Latin *bicŏrnĭa (“anvil”), from Latin bicornis (“two-horned”), from bi- (“two”) + cornī (“horns”), nominalized in the feminine with -a. Cognate with Spanish bigornia, Galician bigorna, French bigorne, early modern Italian bicornia, Andalusian Arabic, Moroccan Arabic, and Algerian Arabic

parole.significato: yawn (open the mouth and take a deep breath)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *buccidiāre, formed from bucca (“mouth”), thus related to modern boca (“mouth”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese buxeta, from Vulgar Latin *buxita, from Late Latin buxis, borrowed from Ancient Greek πυξίς (puxís, “box”), from πῠ́ξος (pŭ́xos, “boxwood”) + -ῐς (-ĭs, feminine suffix). Doublet of boate and bússola. For the semantic development, compare English box (“vagina”).
From boi + -eiro, possibly corresponding to Vulgar Latin, Late Latin bovārius or boārius (“cow herder”), from Latin bovārius, boārius (“of cattle”), from bōs.

parole.significato: doll (a toy in the form of a human)
parole.testo: Uncertain; see the Galician cognate. Maybe from Vulgar Latin *munnecca, *bunnecca, which also yielded Spanish muñeca, but meanings other than 'doll' (and derivates) don't match.

From Old Galician-Portuguese berbeleta of uncertain origin. Possible etymologies include: * Old Galician-Portuguese *belbeleta, from Vulgar Latin *belbellita, from bellus (“beautiful”). * Vulgar Latin *papilitta, from Latin pāpiliō (“butterfly”). Cognate with Galician bolboreta.

parole.significato: tassel (ball-shaped bunch of plaited or otherwise entangled threads)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *burrula, diminutive of Late Latin burra. Compare Spanish borla.
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Vulgar Latin *pustella, from Latin pustula. Compare Spanish postilla, Asturian postiella.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese braadar, from Vulgar Latin *balatrāre (“to shout, to shriek”), probably related to Latin balatrō (“charlatan”), probably from balō (“to baa”). Cognate with Galician bradar, Spanish baladrar, Catalan baladrejar.

parole.significato: ember (a glowing piece of coal or wood)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese brasa, from Vulgar Latin *brasa, of uncertain origin. Cognate with Fala and Galician brasa.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese bravo, possibly from Vulgar Latin *bravus or *brabus, from a fusion of Latin prāvus and barbarus.

Possibly inherited from Vulgar Latin *bragius, from Ancient Greek βράγος (brágos, “marsh, shallows”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH- (“to dig, bore”); compare Albanian bërrakë. Or, inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese brejo, from Proto-Celtic *bracum (“swamp”), from Proto-Indo-European
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *brigna (“rocky terrain”).
From Vulgar Latin *vrincu, *vincru, *vinclu from Latin vinculum, from vinciō (“bind, fetter, tie”) + -culum. Doublet of vínculo and vinco.
From Vulgar Latin *bucculārius (“bossed”), from Latin buccula (“boss”), diminutive of bucca (“cheeck”), .

parole.significato: pit; hole (hollow spot in a surface)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from Old Galician-Portuguese furaco, through Vulgar Latin *foraculum from Latin forāmen (“aperture, opening”). Compare Galician buraco, furaco, furado, Asturian furacu, buracu, Ladino burako, Leonese buraco, Spanish buraco; compare also, just for the card games, Italian burraco a

parole.significato: hairy, long-haired (having a lot of hair)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cabeludo, from Vulgar Latin *capillūtus. By surface analysis, cabelo (“hair”) + -udo. Compare Spanish cabelludo, Italian capelluto and French chevelu.

parole.significato: cape (piece of land extending beyond the coast)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cabo (“besides; nearby”), from Vulgar Latin capus, from Latin caput (“head”), from Proto-Italic *kaput, from Proto-Indo-European *kauput-. Doublet of caput, chefe, and chef.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cabrito (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria). By surface analysis, cabra + -ito. May have originally corresponded to a Vulgar Latin or Late Latin caprītus (attested in Salic Law), from *caprio (“*caprīre”), from Latin caper (which would have normally yielded
From Vulgar Latin *cacca, cognate with Ancient Greek κάκκη (kákkē, “dung”).

parole.significato: shard; piece (broken piece of ceramic or glass)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *cacculus, from Latin caccabus (“pot”), see also Galician cacho (“broken container, broken piece of a container”) and Spanish cacho.

From Old Galician-Portuguese cadeira, from Vulgar Latin *cathēgra, variant of Latin cathedra, from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra), from κατά (katá, “above”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “chair”). Doublet of cátedra, a borrowing.
From Vulgar Latin *capreus, from Latin caper. Compare Spanish cabrio, cf. also French chevron.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cal, from Vulgar Latin cals, from Latin calx, from Ancient Greek χάλιξ (khálix, “pebble”).
From Vulgar Latin *callāre, from Latin chalāre, from Ancient Greek χαλάω (khaláō).
From Old Galician-Portuguese cãalla, from Vulgar Latin *canālia, from Latin canālis (“gutter, ditch”); cf. cale and canal.
From Old Galician-Portuguese cambiar, from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin cambiāre, from change in conjugation of cambīre, of Gaulish origin. Compare Spanish cambiar.

From Old Galician-Portuguese camelo, from Vulgar Latin *camēllus, from Latin camēlus, from Ancient Greek κάμηλος (kámēlos), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *gamal-. Cognate with Galician camelo and Spanish camello.

parole.significato: to walk (travel a distance by walking)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cammīnāre. By surface analysis, caminho (“path”) + -ar (forms 1st conjugation verbs).
From Vulgar Latin *cannastrum, *cannastra, an alteration of Latin canistrum, from Ancient Greek κάναστρον (kánastron).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese candeeiro (“candelabrum”), from Vulgar Latin *candelārius.

parole.significato: kennel (facility at which dogs are reared or boarded)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *canīle, derived from Latin canis (“dog”). By surface analysis, cão + -il.

parole.significato: to castrate (to remove the testicles of)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese capar, from Vulgar Latin *cappāre, derivative of *cappō, from Latin cāpō.

From Old Galician-Portuguese capon, from a Vulgar Latin root *cappō, *cappōnem, from Latin cāpō, probably from Proto-Indo-European *kop- (“to strike, to beat”). Compare Catalan capó, English capon, French chapon, Italian cappone, Spanish capón.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese caralho. Further etymology is uncertain, but the most plausible source on the basis of both semantics and historical phonology appears to be unattested Vulgar Latin *characulum, which would have been a Latinized diminutive of Ancient Greek χάραξ (khárax, “stick
From Vulgar Latin *carēscere, from Latin carēre (“to lack”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *carnītia, from Latin carō (“meat”).
From Vulgar Latin *carnūtus, derived from Latin carnem (“meat”). By surface analysis, carne + -udo.
From Vulgar Latin *carudium, from Ancient Greek καρύδιον (karúdion), from κάρυον (káruon, “nut”). Cognate with Spanish and Galician carozo.

parole.significato: sedge (any plant of the genus Carex)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese carriço, from Vulgar Latin *cāriceus, from Latin cārex (“sedge”). Cognate with Galician and Spanish carrizo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *quassicāre, frequentative from Latin quassāre (“strike”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese caaveira, from Vulgar Latin *calavaria, from Latin calvāria (“skull”). Doublet of calvária. Cognate with Galician caveira, Spanish and Catalan calavera.
From Old Galician-Portuguese caçar, from Vulgar Latin *captiāre, from Latin captus.

From Old Galician-Portuguese serrar, çerrar, sarrar, çarrar, from Vulgar Latin serrāre (“close, shut”), from Late Latin serāre (“to fasten, to bolt”), from Latin sera (“bolt, cross-bar”). Cognate with Galician and Spanish cerrar, French serrer and Italian serrare.

parole.significato: slaughter; massacre (the killing of a large number of people)
parole.testo: Unknown. Maybe from Vulgar Latin *siccina (“dry meat”), from Latin siccus (“dry”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *flammizāre, from Latin flamma. Derivable from chama (“flame”) + -ejar (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: heathland (tract of scrubland habitats characterised by open, low growing woody vegetation)
parole.testo: Unknown, possibly from Vulgar Latin *cerrica, from cerrus (“Turkey oak”), via Mozarabic.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese chato, from Vulgar Latin *plattus (“flattened”), borrowed from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “wide; broad”). Doublet of prato and plati-. Compare Sicilian chiattu.

parole.significato: drawbar, peg, etc, used to join a plough to a yoke, or in general any two elements together
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *clāvicla, from Latin clāvicula. Compare Galician chavella. Doublet of clavícula, cravelha, and cavilha.

parole.significato: to smell (to perceive a smell with the nose)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cheirar (“to smell”), from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin flagrāre, by dissimilation from Latin fragrāre. Cognate to Galician cheirar, Extremaduran cheral, Catalan and Occitan flairar, Sicilian ciagurari, French flairer, and English flair (through Old French flair).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin suispedem, from suis (“pig”, genitive singular) + pēs (“foot”).

parole.significato: to brood (to keep an egg warm until it hatches)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cloccāre, from Latin glocīre.

parole.significato: cuttlefish (any of various squidlike cephalopod marine mollusks of the genus Sepia)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cluccus, metathesis of *cuclus, from Latin cucullus (“hood”). Compare Galician and Spanish choco.

parole.significato: liquid fat that seeps from meat
parole.testo: Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *florumen, from Latin flos (“flower”). Compare Galician chorima.
From Old Galician-Portuguese chopo, from Vulgar Latin *ploppus, from a metathetical alteration and contraction of Classical Latin pōpulus (“poplar”). Compare Spanish chopo.

parole.significato: to rain (to fall (drops of water) from the sky)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese chover, from Vulgar Latin *plovere, from Classical Latin pluere. Cognate with Galician chover and Spanish llover.
Onomatopoeic or from a Vulgar Latin *suctiare. Compare Italian ciucciare, Venetan ciuciar.
From Vulgar Latin *sufilāre, from Latin sibilāre. By surface analysis, chufa + -ar.

parole.significato: cicada (any of several insects of the order Hemiptera)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cicār(r)a, from Latin cicāda.
From Old Galician-Portuguese cinco~cinquo~cinque, from Vulgar Latin cīnque, from Latin quīnque. Distantly, a doublet of ponche.

From Old Galician-Portuguese cĩisa (“ashes”), from a Vulgar Latin root *cinisia (“ashes (cold or warm)”), from Latin cinis (“cold ashes”), from Proto-Indo-European *ken- (“dust, ashes”). Cognate with Galician cinza, Spanish ceniza and Romanian cenușă.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese *cirurgião, cilurgião, celorgião, *cerorgião (“chirurgeon”), from *chīrūrgiānus, a Vulgar Latin derivative of Latin chīrūrgia (“surgery”), from chīrūrgus (“surgeon”), from Ancient Greek χειρουργία (kheirourgía), from χείρ (kheír, “hand”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”)

parole.significato: to scratch (to excavate with the claws)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *scissicāre, from Latin scindere (“to cut, separate”). By surface analysis, cisco + -ar. The sense relating to unfaithful flirting might be in reference to the slang sense for galinha (“someone who is never single”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *zēlūmen, from Latin zēlus (“rivalry, zeal, jealousy”), from Ancient Greek ζῆλος (zêlos), from Proto-Indo-European *yeh₂-.
From Old Galician-Portuguese coallar, quallar (compare Galician callar), from Vulgar Latin *coāglāre/*quāglāre (compare Spanish cuajar), from Latin coāgulāre. Doublet of coagular, a borrowing.
From Old Galician-Portuguese quallo, from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin quāglum, from Latin coāgulum following syncopation. Doublet of coágulo, which is a borrowing.

parole.significato: snake; serpent (any reptile of the suborder Serpentes)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese coobra, from Vulgar Latin *colŏbra, altered from Classical Latin colubra, feminine counterpart to coluber (“snake”), of uncertain origin. Cognate with Galician cobra and Spanish culebra.

parole.significato: to charge (ask for a certain amount of money for something)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese cobrar, from Vulgar Latin *cuperāre (“take, seize”), a back-formation from Latin recuperāre (“recover, regain”), whence Portuguese recobrar. Doublet of recuperar, a borrowing from Latin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cocicāre, frequentative of coquere (“to cook, to roast”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cucumellus, diminutive of Latin cucuma (“large cooking vessel”). Compare Galician cogomelo, Occitan cocomèla and Sardinian cugumeddu.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese coita, from coitar, from Vulgar Latin *cōctare, from Latin coactus (“forced”). Compare Galician coita and Spanish cuita.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese coitar, from Vulgar Latin *coctāre, from Latin *cōctus, from coactus, past participle of cōgō. Doublet of coagir and unrelated to coito.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin colla, from Ancient Greek κόλλα (kólla, “glue”). Compare Spanish cola, French colle, Italian colla.
From Vulgar Latin coda, from Latin cauda. Doublet of cauda, a borrowing.

From Old Galician-Portuguese colmẽa, inherited from Vulgar Latin *colmēna, from Paleo-Hispanic, most likely from Proto-Celtic *kolmēnā, derived from *kŏlmos (“straw”). Compare Galician colmea and Spanish colmena.
From Vulgar Latin *combattere, from Latin cum + battuō.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese comer, from Vulgar Latin *comēre, restructuring of Latin comedere. Cognate with Galician, Mirandese, Asturian, and Spanish comer and Mirandese quemer.

parole.significato: to start; to begin; to commence
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese começar, from Vulgar Latin *cominitiāre, from com- + Latin initiāre. Compare Galician comezar. It has been supposed that the Portuguese form developed via an unattested *comẽeçar, but this appears unlikely. The loss of /n/ was likely due to analogy with the syn
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Vulgar Latin *compātīscere, from Latin compātī. By surface analysis, com- + padecer (“to suffer”).

parole.significato: crew (especially of a fishing boat); seamanship
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese companha, from Vulgar Latin *compānia, from Late Latin compāniō (whence also French compagnon, Italian compagnone), from cum + pānis. Compare Galician and Spanish compaña.

parole.significato: [with a] to attend, appear, turn up
parole.testo: Probably inherited from Vulgar Latin *compārēscere.
From Old Galician-Portuguese comprar, conprar, from Vulgar Latin *comperāre, from Latin comparāre (“to prepare, to procure, to get, to purchase, to obtain”). Doublet of comparar.
From Vulgar Latin *concla, from Latin conchula, diminutive of concha, from Ancient Greek κόγχη (kónkhē), from Proto-Indo-European *kongʰo-
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese confiar, from Vulgar Latin *cōnfīdāre, from cōnfīdere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cōnfrangere, from Latin cōnfringere.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese conquista, probably deverbal from conquistar. Possibly corresponds to a Vulgar Latin *conquista, from the feminine of Latin conquīsītus.

Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *conquisitāre, from Latin conquisitus, past participle of conquīrō. Displaced Old Galician-Portuguese conquerer. It may also be analyzed as an internal derivative of the past participle of the aforementioned Old Portuguese verb, or an early Romance formation; compare the
From Old Galician-Portuguese [Term?], from Vulgar Latin *cōnsequīre or cōnsequere, from Latin cōnsequī. By surface analysis, con- (“co-”) + seguir (“to follow”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese [Term?], from Vulgar Latin *cōnsertāre, a frequentative verb formed from Latin cōnsertus, perfect passive participle of cōnserō (“fasten, connect, join, bind”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from a Vulgar Latin *cōnstrangere for Latin cōnstringere. Doublet of constringir.

parole.significato: to invite (ask for the presence or participation of someone)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese convidar, from Vulgar Latin *convītāre, from Latin invītāre (“to invite”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese convosco, from con + vosco, the latter from Vulgar Latin vōscum, from Latin vōbīscum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *corem m, from Latin cor n.

From Old Galician-Portuguese coraçon, from Vulgar Latin *corāceōnem, derived from Latin cor, from Proto-Italic *kord, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱḗr ~ *ḱr̥d-. Compare Galician and Spanish corazón, Mozarabic ڧرجون (qurəjūn).
From corcova (“curvature”) + -ar. Alternatively, from Vulgar Latin *concurvāre, from con- + curvāre.
From Old Galician-Portuguese cordeiro, from Vulgar Latin *cordārium, from the Latin agnus cordus (“late-born lamb”).

parole.significato: roe deer (small deer species, Capreolus capreolus)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin curtius, from Latin curtus (“short”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese coser, from Vulgar Latin *cōsēre, from Latin cōnsuere. Compare Galician coser.
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Vulgar Latin *cōnsūtūra, from Latin cōnsūtus, from consuō.

parole.significato: cook (a person who prepares food for a living)
parole.testo: Probably from cozinha + -eiro. Alternatively, inherited from Vulgar Latin *coquīnārium.

parole.significato: to scratch (to rub a surface with a sharp object)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese coçar (“to scratch”), from Vulgar Latin *coctiāre, *cocicāre, from Latin coquere.
From Vulgar Latin *crina, from Latin crinis.

parole.significato: to carry out, to do, to perform
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *complīre, from Latin complēre. The retention of /pl/ is unusual and perhaps reflects some form of conservative tendency. Cf. encher < implēre for the more usual outcome. Compare Galician cumprir, Spanish cumplir.
From Old Galician-Portuguese cunna, cuna, from Vulgar Latin *cunea, from Latin cuneus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ḱū (“sting”). Compare Spanish cuña.
From Old Galician-Portuguese curral, of uncertain origin. Maybe from Vulgar Latin *currālis, from currus (“chariot”). Cognate with Galician curral and Spanish corral.

parole.significato: to tan (to change an animal hide into leather)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *contriō, *conteriō, from Latin conterō (“to grind”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese custar, costar, from Vulgar Latin *cōstāre, from Latin cōnstāre. Doublet of constar, a borrowing.
From Old Galician-Portuguese aca, from Vulgar Latin *eccum hāc. Compare archaic French çà, Spanish acá, Italian qua and Sicilian ccà.

parole.significato: a brook, stream or creek; a small river
parole.testo: From Hispanian Vulgar Latin *corrugus. Cf. Asturian cuérrabu

parole.significato: crust (harder outer layer, especially of bread)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *cutina, from cutis (“skin, rind”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese dançar, from Vulgar Latin *dantiāre.

parole.significato: to thresh (to separate the grain from the straw or husks)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese debullar (compare Galician debullar), from Vulgar Latin *dēpoliāre, from Latin dēspoliāre. Doublet of despojar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dēcadere, from Latin dēcidere.

parole.significato: step (of a staircase) or rung (of a ladder)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese degraao, from Vulgar Latin *dēgradus, from Latin gradus, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰredʰ- (“to walk, go”).

parole.significato: to lie down (to rest in a horizontal position)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese deitar, from a Vulgar Latin *dēctāre, from Latin dējectāre, frequentative of dējicere (“to throw, hurl down”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dēparāre, from de- + parāre (“to prepare”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese depois, depos, from Vulgar Latin dē post. Compare Spanish después, French depuis.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dēretrārius (“last, final”). Compare with French dernier.

parole.significato: to bend, to cause to fall down
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese [Term?], from Vulgar Latin *dērēnāre, from de- (“removal”) + Latin rēn (“kidney”). Akin to Galician derrear. Compare Spanish derrengar.

parole.significato: to bend, to cause to fall down
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *dērēnicāre, from Latin rēnem.
From Vulgar Latin deretēre, from Latin dēterō (“to rub off”). Compare Galician derreter and Spanish derretir.
From des- + afiar, from Vulgar Latin *afidāre (“to trust”). Compare English defy.

parole.significato: to forsake; to abandon; to leave behind (to stop or refrain from supporting)
parole.testo: From des- + amparar, from Vulgar Latin *anteparāre (“to protect, to prepare”), from Latin ante + parō (“to stop, lodge”).
From Vulgar Latin *disdignāre, reshaping of Latin dēdignārī (“disdain, scorn”) from dignārī. Compare Spanish desdeñar, Italian disdegnare, French dédaigner.

From Old Galician-Portuguese desejar; from the noun desejo; cf. Latin dēsīderō, dēsīderāre (“long for, desire, feel the want of, miss, regret”). Possibly corresponds to a Vulgar Latin verb *dēsidiāre, itself perhaps a crossing between Latin dēsīderāre and invidiāre, from invidia. Compare Spanish des

From des- + jejuar, or less likely from a Vulgar Latin *disieiūnāre, from Late Latin ieiūnāre, from Latin ieiūnus. Compare English dine, Catalan dejunar, Spanish desayunar, French déjeuner, Italian digiunare, Occitan dejunar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *deexpetere, from Latin dē- + expetō (“to desire, to strive for”), from petō (“to ask for, to seek”).

parole.significato: to awaken, to wake up (gain consciousness)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese despertar, from earlier espertar, from Vulgar Latin *expertāre, from *expertus, from Latin experrēctus (“awoken”), perfect passive participle of expergīscor (“to awake, to wake up”). Cognate with Galician despertar, espertar, Catalan and Spanish despertar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese desperto, from Vulgar Latin de + * expertus for Latin experrēctus. Compare Spanish despierto.
Likely from Vulgar Latin *districtiāre, from Latin dēstringere.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese dia, from Vulgar Latin *dia, first-declension reshaping of Classical Latin diēs, reformed from the accusative diem, from Proto-Italic *djēm, the accusative of *djous (“day, sky”), from Proto-Indo-European *dyḗws (“heaven, sky”). Distantly related to Deus, Zeus

parole.significato: money (means of exchange and measure of value)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese dĩeiro (a coin of little value), from Vulgar Latin *dīnārius, an alteration of Latin dēnārius (“small Roman silver coin”). Doublet of denário and dinar.

Feminine of direito. Or from Old Galician-Portuguese dereita, feminine form of dereito, from Latin dīrēctus (“straight”), from dīrigō (“lay straight; direct; distribute”), from dis- + regō (“to rule, govern”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ-. Compare Spanish derecha, Catalan dreta, French droite, I

parole.significato: law (body of rules and standards to be applied by courts)
parole.testo: Modified orthographically from Old Galician-Portuguese dereito (compare Spanish derecho), from Vulgar Latin *dērēctus, from Latin dīrēctus. Doublet of direto.
From Old Galician-Portuguese *debãadoira, from Vulgar Latin *dēpānātōria, from Vulgar Latin *dēpānāre. Compare Galician debadoira.

From Old Galician-Portuguese donezỹa (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), from Vulgar Latin *domnicella (“weasel”), reanalyzed as *donic- + -ella, and them suffixed with -inha. Compare Galician denociña.
From Vulgar Latin *domnicellus, possibly through Old Occitan donsel.
From Old Galician-Portuguese donzela, from Vulgar Latin *domnicella, from Latin domina. Compare Old Occitan donçela, Spanish doncella, French demoiselle.
From Old Galician-Portuguese ducea, from a Vulgar Latin *duocina or ducēna, both ultimately from Latin duodecim (“twelve”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese envayr, from Vulgar Latin *invādīre, from Latin invādere (“to invade, to enter”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *imbarricāre, from Latin in- + Vulgar Latin *barra. By surface analysis, embargo + -ar.
Compare Spanish, Galician, and Catalan embriagar. Possibly from Vulgar Latin embriacāre, from Late Latin ēbriācus, from Latin ēbrius.
From Old Galician-Portuguese envurullar, envorullar, from Vulgar Latin *involūcrāre, from Latin involūcrum. By surface analysis, embrulho (“wrap”) + -ar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese empeecer, from Vulgar Latin *impedīscere, inchoative of Latin impedīre. Compare Galician and Spanish empecer

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese emprender, from Vulgar Latin *imprehendere. The current form came from the older emprehender, modified in a learned manner from the popularly inherited, now obsolete, form emprender to more closely reflect the Latin etymon, as with compreender and comprender, r
From Vulgar Latin *incalciāre, derived from Latin calx (“heel”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *incarricāre. By surface analysis, en- + carregar. Compare Spanish encargar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese encontrar, from Vulgar Latin *incontrāre, from Latin in + contrā. Compare Italian incontrare, Old French encontrer, Spanish encontrar.
From Vulgar Latin *indērēctiāre, ultimately from Latin dīrēctus. Compare Italian indirizzare, Catalan endreçar, French adresser, Spanish enderezar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese ãedlo, from Vulgar Latin *anēthulum, diminutive of anēthum, from Ancient Greek ἄνηθον (ánēthon). Cognate with Spanish eneldo.

parole.significato: to swathe (to bind with bandages or rollers)
parole.testo: Probably from en- + faixa + -ar, or less likely a Vulgar Latin *īnfasciāre, from Late Latin fasciāre, from Latin fascia. Compare Spanish fajar, Italian fasciare, Romanian înfășa.

parole.significato: to teach (to pass on knowledge to)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese ensinar, from Vulgar Latin īnsignāre (also found in Medieval Latin), from Latin signāre.
Deverbal from ensinar (“to teach”), from Old Galician-Portuguese ensinar, from Vulgar Latin īnsignō (“to engrave”), Latin signum (“mark”), from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”).

parole.significato: to bury, to inter, to entomb
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese enterrar, from Vulgar Latin *interrāre (“to put into earth”), from Latin terra. By surface analysis, en- + terra + -ar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *intervidēre.
From Old Galician-Portuguese enton, from Vulgar Latin *in tunc, from Latin in + tunc (“then”). Displaced collateral form entonce. Compare Spanish entonces.
From Vulgar Latin *involtus, from *involvitus or *involŭtus, for Latin involūtus. Doublet of involuto.
From Vulgar Latin *asciāta, from Latin ascia. Compare Galician aixada, Spanish azada, and Catalan aixada.

parole.significato: to rinse (to remove soap from something using water)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exaquāre with a change in prefix.

From Old Galician-Portuguese erger, from Vulgar Latin *ergere, from Latin ērigere. The modern verb has been rebuilt around the conjugation ergo (“I raise”), hence the other inflexions now all have /ɡ/ rather than the /ʒ/ one would expect from medieval forms like erger. Galician erguer and Spanish er
From Old Galician-Portuguese escaada, from Vulgar Latin *scālāta, from Latin scāla (“stair, staircase, ladder”).
From Vulgar Latin *excalfāre, from Latin excal(e)facere.

parole.significato: to barter (to exchange goods or services without involving money)
parole.testo: An alteration of escambiar, from Vulgar Latin *excambiāre. By surface analysis, escambo + -ar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excambiāre. By surface analysis, es- + cambiar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese escapar, from Vulgar Latin *excappāre, a verb based on Late Latin cappa (“cloak”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese escasso, from Vulgar Latin *excarsus, for Latin excerptus, from excerpō. Thus doublet of excerto.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese escolher, possibly from a Vulgar Latin *excolligere, from Latin ex- + colligere (“to gather”). Compare Galician escoller, Spanish escoger, Catalan escollir.

parole.significato: to slide (to move on a low friction surface)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese escorregar, from Vulgar Latin *excurricāre.
From Old Galician-Portuguese escrivan, from Vulgar Latin *scrībānem, from alteration of declension from Latin scrība (“writer, scribe”). Doublet of escriba, a borrowing.
From Old Galician-Portuguese esfolar (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), from Vulgar Latin *exfollāre. By surface analysis, es- (“ex-”) + fol (“hide, skin, bag”) + -ar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin exfrīgidāre, from Latin ex- (intensifying prefix) + Late Latin frīgidāre (“to make cold”).

parole.significato: to hone (to refine or master a skill)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *exmerāre (“to purify”), from Latin ex merēre. Compare Spanish esmerar.

parole.significato: to break down, to detail (to explain carefully and in detail)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese, from es- + Vulgar Latin *minūtiāre, derived from Latin minūtus. Compare Galician esmiuzar.

From Vulgar Latin emorescĕre, frequentative of Latin ēmori, ēmorior (“to die (out)”), from Latin morior (“to die”), whence Portuguese morrer (“to die”); but note also Old English smorian (“to choke, suffocate”). Cognate to Galician and Spanish esmorecer.

From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Vulgar Latin *expaventāre, derived from the present participle of Classical Latin expaveō. Compare Spanish and Catalan espantar, Italian spaventare, French épouvanter.
Either from es- + pavor + -ar, or from a Vulgar Latin *expavorīre, from *pavorīre, from pavor. Compare Italian spaurire, Occitan espavordir; cf. also Romanian speria.

parole.significato: mirror (smooth surface, usually made of glass with reflective material painted on the underside)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese espelho, from Vulgar Latin speclum, syncopated form of Latin speculum. Compare Galician espello and Spanish espejo. Doublet of espéculo.

parole.significato: to spy (to act as a spy)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *spiāre, from Gothic or Frankish *spehōn, from Proto-Germanic *spehōną (“to see, look”), from Proto-Indo-European *speḱ- (“to look”).

parole.significato: to peek at; to peer (to observe while hidden)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese espreitar, probably from Vulgar Latin *explicitāre, frequentative of explicāre.

parole.significato: to squeeze (to apply pressure to from two or more sides at once)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *expremere, from Latin exprimere. Doublet of exprimir.
From earlier esqueecer, from Old Galician-Portuguese escaecer, from Vulgar Latin *excadescere, derived ultimately from Latin cadere (“fall”). Compare Galician esquecer.

parole.significato: squirrel (any of the rodents of the family Sciuridae distinguished by their large bushy tail)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *scuriolus, diminutive of scurius, variant of Latin sciurus.

parole.significato: catafalque (platform to display or convey a coffin)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *ersa, past participle of ērigēre (“to erect”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese estabelecer, from Vulgar Latin *stabilēscere, from Latin stabilīre.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese estalar, from Vulgar Latin *astellāre, from Latin astulla, alternative form of assula, from assis (“axis, wheel, axle”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin exterrēscere, frequentative of Latin exterrēre.

parole.significato: rockrose (any of shrub of the genus Cistus), particularly
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *stīpa, from Latin stīpes (“stake”).

parole.significato: to spoil, to damage, to corrupt, to ruin, to break
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese estragar, from Vulgar Latin *strāgāre, from Latin strāgēs (“defeat, slaughter”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese estrondo, probably from a Vulgar Latin *extronitus, or less likely *extronotus, from metathesis of Latin tonitrus (“thunder”). Compare Spanish estruendo.
From Old Galician-Portuguese [Term?], from Vulgar Latin strumen, alteration of Latin strāmen (“straw for bedding”). Compare Galician estrume.
From Vulgar Latin *exvānĕre, from Latin vānus. Cf. also French évanouir, Old French esvanir.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fascŭlō, from fax (“torch”). Compare Galician facho.

From Old Galician-Portuguese fada, from Vulgar Latin *Fāta (“goddess of fate”), from the plural of Latin fātum (“fate”). Compare Galician, Catalan, and Occitan fada, Spanish hada, French fée and Italian fata.
From Old Galician-Portuguese fagulla, from a Vulgar Latin root *facucla, from syncopation of *facucula, from Latin facula. Doublet of fácula, a borrowing, and of facha. Compare Sicilian faviḍḍa.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese falescer, derived from falir, from Vulgar Latin *fallīre, from Latin fallere. Cognate with Galician falecer, Spanish fallecer.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese falir, from Vulgar Latin *fallīre, from Classical Latin fallere, possibly from Proto-Italic *falsō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)gʷʰh₂el-.

parole.significato: lack (the condition of not having, needing, or needing more of something)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese falta, from Vulgar Latin *fallita, feminine of *fallitus, in place of Latin falsus, perfect passive participle of fallō. Cognate to Catalan falta, English fault, Spanish falta and French faute.
From earlier famiinto, from Old Galician-Portuguese famĩento, from Vulgar Latin *faminentus, from Latin famēs (“hunger”). Cognate with Galician famento and Spanish hambriento.
From Vulgar Latin *farellum, from Latin far (“spelt”). Cognate with Galician farelo and Asturian fariellu.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fechar (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), from Vulgar Latin pesclum, from Latin pessulus (“bolt”). Probably a southern Portuguese variant, with the change of /p/ to /f/ reflecting Arabic influence. By surface analysis, fecho + -ar.
From Vulgar Latin *foeticosus, from foetidus.
From Old Galician-Portuguese fel, from Vulgar Latin *felem m or f, from Latin fel n.
From Old Galician-Portuguese ferido, from Vulgar Latin *ferītus (“stricken”), perfect passive participle of feriō (“to strike”).

parole.significato: tool (mechanical device intended to make a task easier)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Vulgar Latin ferrāmenta, from the plural of Latin ferrāmentum.

parole.significato: bolt (sliding pin or bar in a lock)
parole.testo: From a modification of Old Galician-Portuguese verrolho (influenced by ferro (“iron”)), from Vulgar Latin *verruculum, from Latin vericulum, diminutive of verū (“dart”). Compare development of Spanish cerrojo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *festizāre. Derivable from festa + -ejar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fiar, from Vulgar Latin *fīdāre, from Latin fīdere. Compare Galician and Spanish fiar.

parole.significato: to become; to get; to end up
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese ficar (also fincar), from Vulgar Latin *fīg(i)cāre, frequentative based on Latin fīgere (“drive in, fix in place”). Doublet of fincar.

parole.significato: a traditional christmas treat prepared with eggs and flour, fried in olive oil; beignet, fritter
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese folloa, from Vulgar Latin *foliola, diminutive of Latin folium. Compare Galician filloa, Spanish hojuela.
From Vulgar Latin *filōlum, diminutive of Latin filum.

From Old Galician-Portuguese fincar, from Vulgar Latin *fīg(i)cāre, frequentative based on Latin fīgere (“drive in, fix in place”). Doublet of ficar. The -n- may be due to the influence of Latin fingere and its derivatives.
From Old Galician-Portuguese fĩidar, from Vulgar Latin *fīnītāre, from Latin fīnītus, perfect passive participle of fīnīō.
From Old Galician-Portuguese firme, from Vulgar Latin firmis, from Latin firmus, from Proto-Italic *fermos, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰer-mo-s (“holding”), from the root *dʰer- (“to hold”).

parole.significato: to stare at; to gaze at
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *fictāre, from Latin fictum (“fixed”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese fivela, from Vulgar Latin *fībella, diminutive of Latin fībula (whence Portuguese fíbula was borrowed). Cognate with Galician fibela and Spanish hebilla.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *folliclu, from Latin folliculus, doublet of folículo. Compare Spanish hollejo.
From formiga (“ant”) + -eiro; possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *formīcārium, from Latin formīca. Compare Spanish hormiguero, Catalan formiguer, Italian formicaio, Romanian furnicar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese forçar, from Vulgar Latin *fortiāre, from Late Latin fortia, from Latin fortis. By surface analysis, força + -ar. Compare Galician forzar.

From Old Galician-Portuguese fraga (compare Galician fraga), from Iberian Vulgar Latin fraga, plural of fragum (compare also Catalan and Occitan frau), from fragōsus (“rough”), from fragor, from frangō (“break, shatter”); cf. also Latin fragilis.

parole.significato: regular (frequent customer, client or business partner)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese feegres, from Vulgar Latin fīl(ius) ecclēsiae (“son of the church”). Cognate with Galician fregués and Spanish feligrés.
From Old Galician-Portuguese fresco, from Vulgar Latin *friscum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *frigorentus. Compare Spanish friolento.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *frīctūra. By surface analysis, fritar + -ura.

From Old Galician-Portuguese frauga, from a Vulgar Latin *frabica, a metathetic form of Latin fabrica (“smithy, forge”). Doublet of the borrowing fábrica and of forja, from French. Cognate with Galician frágoa, frauga, Spanish fragua.

parole.significato: likely or tending to run away
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *fugītīcius, from Latin fugere (“flee”). By surface analysis, fugido + -iço.

parole.significato: to run away; to flee (to move away from something unpleasant quickly or suddenly)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese fugir, from Vulgar Latin *fugīre, from Latin fugere, from Proto-Italic *fugiō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewg-. Cognate with Galician fuxir, Asturian afuxir, Catalan fugir, Italian fuggire, French fuir, Spanish huir.
From Old Galician-Portuguese fuuncho, feuncho, from Vulgar Latin *fēnuclum, from Late Latin fēnuculum (“fennel”), a diminutive of Latin fēnum. Compare Galician fiúncho, also fiollo, Spanish hinojo.

parole.significato: greyhound (lean breed of dog used in hunting and racing)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese galgo, from Vulgar Latin Gallicus (canis) (“French (dog)”), from Gallia (“Gaul, modern-day France”). Doublet of gálico.

parole.significato: gall (tumorous growth on the surface of plants)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *gallea, from Latin galla.

parole.significato: branch (woody part of a tree arising from the trunk and usually dividing)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *galleus (“oaken”), from Latin galla (“oak apple”).

parole.significato: fallow deer (Dama dama, a ruminant mammal)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *gammus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ganantiam.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *gemellicum, from Latin gemellus, from geminus. Compare Galician xemelgo, Asturian ximielgu and Spanish mielgo.
From Vulgar Latin *gulella, diminutive of Latin gula.
From Vulgar Latin or Late Latin colfus, colphus, culfus, alteration of colpus, from Ancient Greek κόλπος (kólpos).

parole.significato: aquamanile (water vessel used to wash the hands)
parole.testo: From agomil, from Vulgar Latin *aquiminīle or *aquaminīle, from Late Latin aquamanīle, from Latin aqua (“water”) and the root of manus (“hand”). Compare Spanish aguamanil.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *grānicium or from grão (“grain”) + -iço. Compare Galician greiza.

From Old Galician-Portuguese gralla, from a Vulgar Latin root *gracla, syncopated form of Late Latin grācula, from Latin grāculus, from Proto-Indo-European *greh₂-k- (“croak”). Compare Spanish grajo, graja, Catalan gralla, Italian gracchia.

From Old Galician-Portuguese grallo, from Vulgar Latin *graclu(s), syncopated form of Latin grāculus (“jackdaw”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *greh₂-k- (“croak”). Compare Spanish grajo, Italian gracchio.

parole.significato: to quack (to make a noise like a duck)
parole.testo: From Iberian Vulgar Latin *gracināre, from Latin crocitāre, ultimately onomatopoeic.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *crassia.

parole.significato: to shout, to scream, to yell
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *crītāre.
From Vulgar Latin *werrizāre. Derivable from guerra (“war”) + -ear (verb-forming suffix).

From Old Galician-Portuguese yrto, from Vulgar Latin *erctus, vernacular variant of Classical Latin ērēctus, therefore a doublet of ereto. Despite the resemblance, unlikely to derive from Latin hirtus (“shaggy”). Compare Galician irto, Spanish yerto.

parole.significato: flank (flesh between the last rib and the hip)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese yllarga, from Vulgar Latin *īliārica, from Latin īlia, plural of īle (“guts, intestines”). Cognate with Spanish ijar (“flank”).
From a semi-learned modification of Old Galician-Portuguese ẽemizade (based on inimigo), from Vulgar Latin *inimīcitātem, from Latin inimīcus, based on inimīcitia. Compare Spanish enemistad.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese janella, from Vulgar Latin *iānuella, diminutive of Latin iānua (“door”). Etymology 1, noun sense 3 and etymology 1, noun sense 4 are semantic loans from English window. Compare Galician xanela, Mirandese jinela. Related to Mozarabic יאנה (yʔnh).
From Old Galician-Portuguese jantar, jentar (“lunch, to have lunch”), from Vulgar Latin *iantāre (“to eat lunch”), from Latin ientāre (“to breakfast”). See iēntāculum (“the first meal of the day”).

parole.significato: way, manner, fashion (how something is done)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese geito, from a Vulgar Latin *iectus, alteration of Latin iactus. Compare Galician xeito. Doublet of jato.
From Vulgar Latin *iolium, from Latin lolium. Compare Spanish joyo and Catalan jull.
Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *labrar, from Latin labōrāre.

parole.significato: to tear up (have watery eyes before crying)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *lacrimizāre. The reason for there being a /k/ instead of the expected */ɡ/ (cf. lágrima) is not apparent.
From Vulgar Latin *lacarta, from Latin lacerta. Mostly displaced the inherited eruga, from Latin eruca (“caterpillar”).

parole.significato: wall lizard (reptile of the family Lacertidae)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese lagarto, from Vulgar Latin *lacartum, from Latin lacertus, of uncertain origin.
From Old Galician-Portuguese lagosta, from Vulgar Latin lacusta, from Latin locusta, of uncertain origin.
From Vulgar Latin labōria (“work, labour”), from Latin labōrāre (“to work”).

parole.significato: to lasso (to capture with a lasso)
parole.testo: From laço (“lasso; lace”) + -ar, from Old Galician-Portuguese laço, from Vulgar Latin *laceus, from Latin laqueus (“noose; snare”).

parole.significato: any type of tie that is easily undone
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese laço, from Vulgar Latin *laceus, from Latin laqueus (“noose; snare”).
From a Vulgar Latin *glirionem, from Latin glīs, glīris. Compare Spanish lirón, French liron.

From Old Galician-Portuguese lentilha (compare Galician lentella), from Vulgar Latin *lenticla (compare Spanish lenteja, Catalan llentilla), from syncopation of Latin lenticula (“lentil”), diminutive of lēns (“lentil bean”). Compare lentícula, a borrowed doublet; cf. also lenticela.
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Vulgar Latin *lĭmăcem, from Latin līmācem.
From Vulgar Latin *levātīcius, from Latin levāre. By surface analysis, levado + -iço.

parole.significato: to stand up; to get up (to rise from a lying, sitting or fallen position)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese levantar, itself from a Vulgar Latin *levantāre, from Latin levantem, present participle of levō. Compare Spanish levantar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese linguainça, from Latin lūcānica, probably through a Vulgar Latin form *lucanicia. Compare Galician longaínza and Spanish longaniza.
Uncertain, possibly from Vulgar Latin *lixāre (“to boil”); compare Late Latin ēlixō (“to boil thoroughly”). Compare Spanish lijar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese *lontra, from a Vulgar Latin variant of Latin lutra. First attested in Gil Vicente's Auto das Fadas. Cf. also Old Galician-Portuguese luntria, attested in 1253.

parole.significato: bay (Laurus nobilis, a shrub of the Mediterranean)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese loureiro, from Vulgar Latin *laurārius, from Latin laurus. By surface analysis, louro (“laurel, laurel leaf”) + -eiro.
From Old Galician-Portuguese luzir, from Vulgar Latin *lūcīre from Latin lūcēre.
From Old Galician-Portuguese levedo, from Vulgar Latin *levĭtum (“yeast, sourdough”), from Latin levātus (“lifted”). Compare Galician lévedo, Spanish leudo.

parole.significato: axe (tool and weapon consisting of a heavy blade on the end of a shaft)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese machado, from Latin marculātus, from marculus (“hammer”).

parole.significato: male (belonging or referring to the sex having the smaller gametes)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese macho, from Vulgar Latin masclus. Doublet of másculo.
From Old Galician-Portuguese maciço, from Vulgar Latin *massīcius. By surface analysis, massa + -iço. Compare Spanish macizo. Doublet of massivo.
From Old Galician-Portuguese madrugar, madurgar, from Vulgar Latin *mātūricāre, derived from Latin mātūrāre (“hurry”) (whence Portuguese madurar).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *manitia, from Latin manus (“hand”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *madiga, from Latin magida, from Ancient Greek μαγίδα (magída).
From Vulgar Latin *macla, from Latin macula (“stain”). Compare the doublets mancha, malha, mácula, mágoa, and mangra.
From Vulgar Latin *mancipius (“slave”), from Latin mancipium (“purchase property”), also "a bought slave". For sense "coatrack" compare English valet.

parole.significato: stain, blemish, mark, spot (discoloured spot or visible impression)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *macla (probably through a variant with a nasal infix *mancla), from Latin macula (“stain, spot”). Doublet of the borrowed terms mácula, malha, mágoa, mangra, and maquis.
From Vulgar Latin *manclāre, *maclāre, from Latin maculāre. Doublet of magoar and macular.

parole.significato: manner; way (particular method of doing something)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese maneira, from Vulgar Latin *manāria, from feminine of Latin manuārius (“relating to the hand”), from manus (“hand”); corresponding to mão + -eira. Compare Galician maneira, Spanish and Catalan manera, French manière, English manner, Romanian mâner.

parole.significato: mildew (growth of minute fungi on plants)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *macla, from Latin macula (“blemish”), probably via Spanish mangla. Doublet of mancha, malha, mágoa, mácula, and maquis.

parole.significato: act (a display of behaviour meant to deceive)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese manna, from Vulgar Latin *mania (“manual skill”), from Latin manus (“hand”). Cognate with Galician and Spanish maña.

From Old Galician-Portuguese mannãa (“morning”), from Vulgar Latin *maneāna (“morning”), from Latin māne (“in the morning”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂- (“to ripen, to mature”). Cognate with Galician mañá, Asturian mañana, Leonese mañana, Mirandese manhana, Spanish mañana, and Aragonese manyana.
From Vulgar Latin *mānsus, from Latin mānsuetus.
Deverbal from mascavar (“to adulterate, to lessen”), corrupted from menoscabar, from Vulgar Latin *minuscapāre.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mazela, from Vulgar Latin macella, diminutive of macula (“spot, stain”). Cognate with Spanish mancilla.

From Old Galician-Portuguese maçãa, from Vulgar Latin māla Mattiāna (literally “apples of Mattium”) though some theorize that Mattiāna was an Iberian pronunciation of the Gallo-Roman word matianium, a golden apple named after Gaius Matius, a horticulturist and friend of Caesar. Cognate with Galician
From Old Galician-Portuguese mederoso, medoroso, from Vulgar Latin *metōrōsum, derived from Latin metus (“fear”, noun).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mel m, from Vulgar Latin *melem m or f, from Latin mel n. Cognates include Galician mel m and Spanish miel f.
From Vulgar Latin *minuscapāre.

parole.significato: to trade (to buy and sell goods)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese mercar (“to trade; to buy”), from Vulgar Latin *mercāre, from Latin mercārī (“to trade”), from merx (“merchandise”), possibly from Etruscan [Term?].
From Vulgar Latin *merēscere, from Latin merēre.

parole.significato: to submerge (to go down in water)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese mergullar, from Vulgar Latin *merguliāre, from Latin mergulus, diminutive of mergus (“diver; loon”), from mergō (“to dive, to plunge”). Cognate with Galician mergullar. Compare also Spanish somorgujar.

From Old Galician-Portuguese mesa (“table”), from Vulgar Latin mēsa, from Latin mēnsa (“table”). Cognate with Galician mesa, Spanish mesa, French moise, Italian mensa and Romanian masă. Not related to Persian میز (mêz, “table”). As both it and Portuguese mesa have been borrowed into different langua

From Old Galician-Portuguese mesmo, from earlier Old Galician-Portuguese meesmo, from Vulgar Latin of Iberia *medesmo, from proto-Romanic forms as *medessimu, from *medissimu, from *medipsimu, from Vulgar Latin *metipsimus, from a previous *metipsissīmus, derived from Latin -met (emphatic suffix) +

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mixillon, from Vulgar Latin *muscelliō (“mussel”), from Latin muscellus, from Latin musculus (“muscle, mussel”). Cognate of Galician mexillón and of Spanish mejillón (“mussel”).

parole.significato: crumb (small piece of bread, biscuit, cake, etc)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese *migalla, from Vulgar Latin *mīcacula, diminutive from Latin mīca (“crumb”). Synchronically miga + -alha.
From Old Galician-Portuguese mejar, from Vulgar Latin *mēiāre, from Latin mēiere. Compare Galician mexar and Spanish mear.

parole.significato: covered with or impregnated with liquid; wet
parole.testo: Past participle of molhar, from Vulgar Latin *molliāre, from Latin mollīre. Compare Spanish mojado, Galician mollado, Catalan mullat, Occitan molhat, French mouillé.
From Old Galician-Portuguese mollar, from Vulgar Latin *molliāre (“soak”), a verb based on Latin mollis (“soft”). Compare Galician mollar, Spanish mojar.
Deverbal from molhar (“to wet; to water”), from Old Galician-Portuguese mollar, from Vulgar Latin *molliāre (“to soak”), from Latin mollis (“soft”), from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥dus (“soft, weak”).

parole.significato: bat (any flying mammal of the order Chiroptera)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese murcego, from Vulgar Latin *mūrem caecus, by surface analysis, mure (“mouse”) + cego (“blind”). Compare Galician morcego, Spanish murciélago.

parole.significato: gag (object placed in someone’s mouth to prevent them from speaking and biting)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mordacia, from Latin mordāx, mordācia (“biting”). Compare Spanish mordaza and Italian mordacchia.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *murrum (“muzzle, snout”).

parole.significato: a landform with elevation intermediate between that of a hill and that of a small mountain
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *murrum, *morrum (“mound, hillock”), cognate with Occitan morre.

From Old Galician-Portuguese morto, from Vulgar Latin *mortu(s), from Latin mortuus, perfect active participle of morior (“to die”). Corresponds to Proto-Indo-European *mr̥twós, *mr̥tós (“dead, mortal”), *mr̥tó-, ultimately from *mer- (“to die”). Compare Galician morto and Spanish muerto.

parole.significato: Sorbus spp., especially common whitebeam (Aria edulis, syn. Sorbus aria)
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin extension of Latin mustum (“must”), because of the berries being stored in must or tasting of wine. See Arabic مُشْتَهَى (muštahā) for cognates.

From Old Galician-Portuguese mõesteiro (“monastery”), from Vulgar Latin *monistērium from Late Latin monastērium (“monastery, monk's cell”), from Ancient Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion, “hermit's cell”), from μόνος (mónos, “alone”). Cognate with Galician mosteiro, English minster and French moutier
From Vulgar Latin *movitīcius, from Latin movēre (“move”). Compare Spanish movedizo, Catalan movedís.
From Vulgar Latin mungere, from Classical Latin mulgēre (“to milk”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *h₂melǵ-.

Probably from Vulgar Latin *mustidus (“wet”), from Latin mustum (“unfermented wine”) and related to muscum (“moss”); from Proto-Indo-European *mus-, *mews- (“damp”). Cognate with Galician murcho, Spanish mustio, and Old Occitan moste.
From Old Galician-Portuguese marmor, from Vulgar Latin *marmŏrem, from Latin marmor n, from Ancient Greek μάρμαρος (mármaros, “marble”).

parole.significato: having a big or long nose
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *nārīcūtus, ultimately derived from Latin nāris. By surface analysis, nariz + -udo.

parole.significato: nostril (either of the two orifices located on the nose)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *narina, from Latin nāris (“nostril”), from nāsus (“nose”), from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s. Cognate with Spanish narina, and French narine.

From Old Galician-Portuguese navalla, inherited from Vulgar Latin *navac(u)la, from Latin novācula (“a sharp knife, dagger, razor”). Doublet of novácula. Cognate with Catalan and Galician navalla, Mirandese nabalha and Spanish navaja.

parole.significato: to snow (to have snow fall from the sky)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese nevar, from Vulgar Latin *nevāre, ultimately from Latin nivem (“snow”, noun). By surface analysis, neve (“snow”) + -ar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese neve, from Vulgar Latin *nĕvem, alteration of Latin nivem.

From Old Galician-Portuguese noa, from earlier Old Galician-Portuguese nõa, from Vulgar Latin of Iberia *nona, from proto-Romanic *nona, from Vulgar Latin *nona, from Latin nōna, feminine of nōnus (“ninth”). Doublet of Portuguese, Galician, Spanish, and Italian nona (“ninth”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese novia, from a Vulgar Latin root novia, from Latin nova, possibly influenced by nupta. Compare Spanish novia.
From Old Galician-Portuguese novio, from Vulgar Latin *novius, from Latin novus (“new”). Compare with the Spanish novio.
From Old Galician-Portuguese nora (“daughter-in-law”), from Vulgar Latin *nŏra, from Late Latin nura, from Classical Latin nurus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *snusós.

From Old Galician-Portuguese noveenta, novaenta, from Vulgar Latin *nōvāgintā, from Latin nōnāgintā (blended with novem (“nine”)), from earlier *nūnāgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥(d)ḱomt (“nine tens”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese noze, noce, from earlier *notze, from Vulgar Latin *nŏcem (pronounced nódzie), alteration of Classical Latin nucem (accusative of nux).

parole.significato: cloud (mass of dust, steam or smoke)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese nuve, nuven, from a Vulgar Latin root *nūbinem, from Latin nūbes. Compare Spanish nube.
From Old Galician-Portuguese obedecer, from Vulgar Latin *oboedēscere, from Latin oboedīre.
Derived from Old Galician-Portuguese oferir, from Vulgar Latin *offerīre, from Latin offerre.
From Vulgar Latin *oculāta, ultimately from Latin oculus (“eye”). Compare Catalan ullada or Italian occhiata. Or by surface analysis, olho + -ada.
From Old Galician-Portuguese aollar, from Vulgar Latin *adoculāre, from oclus, from Latin oculus. Cognate with Galician ollar, Mirandese oulhar, Spanish aojar and Italian adocchiare.

parole.significato: to wave (to cause to move back and forth or up and down repeatedly)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *undizāre. Derivable from onda + -ear.

parole.significato: to milk (to express milk from mammal)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese ordennar, from Vulgar Latin *ōrdiniāre, itself from Latin ōrdināre (or through a *ōrdinium), from ōrdō (“order, arrangement”), from Proto-Italic *ored(h)- (“to arrange”), of unknown origin. Compare Spanish ordeñar. Doublet of ordenar.
From Vulgar Latin *orula, diminutive of Latin ora. Compare French orle.

parole.significato: third-person plural direct objective personal pronoun; them
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese os, from Vulgar Latin *los, from Latin illōs.

parole.significato: margin, border, edge, rim (especially of fabric)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *orula, diminutive of ora.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ŏva f sg (“roe”), from Latin ōva n pl (“eggs”). Doublet of ovo (“egg”), from the Latin singular ōvum. Compare Spanish hueva.
From ovo + -ar, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *ōvāre, from Latin ōvum.

parole.significato: egg (cell that results from the fertilization of the female gamete by the male gamete)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ovo, from Vulgar Latin *ŏvum, from Classical Latin ōvum. Doublet of ova.
From Old Galician-Portuguese padecer, presumably derived via some (unattested?) derivative of Vulgar Latin *patīre, from Latin patī. Compare Spanish padecer.

parole.significato: baker (person who bakes and sells bread)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese pãadeiro, from Vulgar Latin pānātārius, from Latin pānis (“bread”).

Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *palātārem, derived from Latin palātum. Considering its intervocalic /l/, presumably borrowed via Spanish paladar. Doublet of padar (the inherited counterpart); cf. also Galician padal.

parole.motivo_incerta: Possibly; modificatore <unc> nel legame; nodo incerto nell'albero
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese panela, from Vulgar Latin *pannella, from Late Latin panna, possibly from Latin patina (“frying pan”). Related to English pan. Cognate with Sicilian panneḍḍa.
From Vulgar Latin parietinariu, from Latin parietina (“old or ruined wall”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese parecer, from Vulgar Latin *pārēscere, from Latin pārēre.

parole.significato: to pass; to pass by (to move past)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese passar, from Vulgar Latin *passāre. Compare Galician and Spanish pasar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese *pata, fom Vulgar Latin *patta (“paw, foot”).

parole.significato: fuse (cord used to ignite a charge)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese pavio, from Vulgar Latin *papīlum, from Latin papȳrus. Doublet of papiro.
From Vulgar Latin *pavōrōsum, derived from Latin pavōrem (“fear”, noun). By surface analysis, pavor + -oso.

parole.significato: to ask for; to request (to express the need or desire for something)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese pedir, from Vulgar Latin *petīre, from Latin petere (“ask, request”). Compare Romanian peți, Italian pezzire.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese *pega, from Vulgar Latin peca, from Latin pīca (“magpie”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)peyk- (“woodpecker; magpie”).

parole.significato: fetter (object used to bind a person or animal by its legs)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese pea, from Vulgar Latin *pedea, from Latin pēdica.
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Vulgar Latin *pectorīlis, from Latin pectus (“chest”). Compare Spanish pretil.

parole.significato: a branch municipal administration in Portugal
