From Old Galician-Portuguese pennor, from Vulgar Latin *pignorem, from Latin pignus n (“pledge”).
From Vulgar Latin *pectinī̆culum, diminutive of Latin pecten (“pubic hair, comb”). By surface analysis, pente + -elho. Compare Galician pentello, Spanish pendejo.

parole.motivo_incerta: Probably; modificatore <unc> nel legame; nodo incerto nell'albero
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese pequeno, probably from Vulgar Latin *peccuinnus. Compare Spanish pequeño, French petit and Italian piccolo.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese pera, from Vulgar Latin *pira, from the plural of Latin pirum, reanalyzed as a feminine singular.
From Vulgar Latin percursus, nominalised past participle of percurrere. Compare French parcours. Doublet of parkour.
From Old Galician-Portuguese perda, from Vulgar Latin *perdita, from the feminine of Latin perditus (“lost”), perfect passive participle of perdō (“to lose”).
Metathesis of preguntar, inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese preguntar, from Vulgar Latin *praecūnctāre, alteration of Latin percontārī.
From Old Galician-Portuguese permanescer, from a Vulgar Latin *permanēscere, an inchoative of Latin permanēre.
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Vulgar Latin *persequīre, from Latin persequor.

parole.significato: to belong (to be property (of); to be owned (by))
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese pertẽecer, from Vulgar Latin *pertinēscēre, from Latin pertinēre, from per (“through”) + teneō (“to hold”). Compare Spanish pertenecer.

parole.significato: weight (force on an object due to the gravitational attraction)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese peso, from Vulgar Latin *pēsum, from Latin pēnsum, from the verb penso (“to weigh”).

parole.significato: venom (animal toxin delivered by a bite or sting)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese peçonna, poçonna, poçõya, from Vulgar Latin *potionea, from Latin pōtiō (“drink”). Cognate of Spanish ponzoña, Galician pezoña and French poison. Doublet of poção.

parole.significato: to sting (pierce with a small, sharp point)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *pīccāre (“to puncture”), itself from *pīccus (“woodpecker”), variant of Latin pīcus, or perhaps a Frankish borrowing.

parole.significato: pillar (large post, often used as supporting architecture)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pīlāre, from Latin pīla (“pillar”).
From Vulgar Latin *pendicāre, from Latin pendere (“to hang”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese pisar, from Vulgar Latin *pisāre, from Latin pīnsāre (“to pound”), from Proto-Indo-European *peys- (“to crush”).

parole.significato: to be able to; can (to have the ability to)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese poder, from Vulgar Latin potēre, regularization of Latin posse.
From Old Galician-Portuguese pois, from Vulgar Latin *pos, from Classical Latin post (“after”). Compare with French puis, Spanish pues, Italian poi, and Romanian apoi (from ad post).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *podiāre.
From Old Galician-Portuguese *poldro, from Vulgar Latin *pulliter. Doublet of potro.

parole.significato: American or English inch, a unit of length equal to 2.54 cm
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese polegada, from Vulgar Latin *pollicāta, unit of length derived from Latin pollex (“thumb”). Compare Galician and Spanish pulgada. As an English unit, a calque of English inch.

parole.significato: orchard (land for cultivation of fruit or nut trees)
parole.testo: Possibly from Vulgar Latin *pomāre, from Latin pomārium, from pōmum (“fruit”). By surface analysis, pomo + -ar.

From Old Galician-Portuguese popa, from Vulgar Latin *puppa, from Latin puppis (“stern”), possibly with influence from prora (“prow”).

parole.significato: why, what for, for what reason (introduces a question)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese porque, from Vulgar Latin [Term?]. By surface analysis, por (“for”) + que (“that”). Doublet of porque. Cognate with Spanish por qué, French pourquoi, Italian perché.

parole.significato: because (introduces a reason for that described in the previous clause)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese porque, from Vulgar Latin [Term?]. By surface analysis, univerbation of por (“for”) + que (“that”). Doublet of por que. Cognate with Galician and Spanish porque, Catalan perquè, French parce que and Italian perché.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese, from Vulgar Latin *pulliter, of dubious deeper etymology, probably derived from Latin pullus. Doublet of poldro.

From Vulgar Latin *plica, from Latin plicō (“to fold”). Doublet of plica.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese prenhe (“pregnant”), from Vulgar Latin *praegnis (“pregnant”), from Latin praegnās (“pregnant”). Cognate with Galician preñe.

parole.significato: dry-cured ham; thigh of a hog cured for food
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *persunctu, ultimately from Classical Latin suctus, perfect passive participle of sugō. Doublet of prosciutto.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pugia, from Latin pungō (“to prick, to puncture, to sting”). Cognate with Galician puga, púa and Spanish púa. The sense "womanizer", "player" is influenced by English PUA.

parole.significato: flea (a small, wingless, parasitic insect of the order Siphonaptera, renowned for its bloodsucking habits and jumping a…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese pulga, from the hypothetical Vulgar Latin *pūlica, from Latin pūlex (“flea”), from Proto-Indo-European *plus- (“flea”).

parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *pūtta, of uncertain origin, perhaps derived from Latin *puta, female form of Latin putus (“teeny boy”), a hapax legomenon of dubious reading. parole.significato: passerine (any bird of the order Passeriformes)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese passaro, from Vulgar Latin *passarum, from Latin passer (“sparrow”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *p(e)t-tro- (“who flies, bird”), from *peth₂- (“to fly”). Compare English passerine, Spanish pájaro, Dalmatian paserain, Romanian pasăre.

From Vulgar Latin *crepantāre, derived from Latin crepere (“rattle”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese quedar, from Vulgar Latin quētāre, from Late Latin quiētāre (“to quiet”), from Latin quietārī. Compare Portuguese borrowed doublet quietar. See also quitar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese queimar, from Vulgar Latin *caimāre, a Greek-influenced modification of Latin cremāre. Compare Galician queimar, Spanish quemar.

parole.significato: any animal of the Tayassuidae family (a wild pig family of the Americas)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese queixada (“jaw”), from Vulgar Latin *capseāta, a derivative of Vulgar Latin *capseus (“chin”) (whence queixo), itself a derivative of Latin capsa (“box”), from capiō (“capture, seize, take”), from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to take, seize, catch, grasp”). Inherited from Vulgar Latin *quassiāre, from Latin quassāre (“to shake”). Compare Spanish quejar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese queixo, from Vulgar Latin *capseum, from Latin capsa (“box”).

parole.significato: yard (land with vegetable garden, next to a house)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese quintãal, from Vulgar Latin *quintanālem; equivalent to quinta + -al.

From Vulgar Latin *rabulāre.

parole.significato: to creak (to make a prolonged sharp squeaking sound)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese renger, from Vulgar Latin *ringīre, from Latin ringor (“to show one's teeth”). Cognate with Galician renxer (“creak, grind (one's teeth)”).

parole.significato: to scrape (draw a sharp object along a surface)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese rascar, from Vulgar Latin *rāsicāre, a frequentative verb based on Latin rāsus (“shaven”).

parole.significato: to scrape (draw a sharp object along a surface)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *raspāre, from Frankish *hraspōn.

parole.significato: rat (any rodent of the genus Rattus)

From Old Galician-Portuguese recado, from recadar, from Vulgar Latin *recapitō.

parole.significato: to dig out (vines) again to clear them of weeds

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *recaptiāre.

parole.significato: to reiterate (to say or do something for a second time)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *reiterāre, from Latin re- (“re-”) + iterāre (“to repeat”).

From Vulgar Latin *rehinnitulāre, from Latin hinnitŭlus or hinnītus, perfect passive participle of hinniō (“to neigh”). Cognate of Galician rinchar.
From remanescer (“to remain”) + -ente (“-ent”), from Vulgar Latin *remanēscō (“to remain”), from Latin remaneō (“to remain behind; to endure”).

Relatinized from Old Galician-Portuguese resprandecer, from Vulgar Latin *resplandēscere, from Latin resplendēscere, from re + splendēscere.

parole.significato: to laugh (to express mirth or derision by emitting chuckling sounds)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese riir, from Vulgar Latin *rīdīre, from Latin rīdēre.

parole.significato: to cover with rattle; to dew
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rōscidāre, derived from Latin rōscidus. Compare Spanish rociar, Catalan ruixar.

parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *rubeolum, from rubellus (“reddish”).

parole.significato: to follow (to go or come after in physical space)

From Old Galician-Portuguese semellar, from Vulgar Latin *similiāre, a verb derived from Latin similis (“similar”). Compare Galician semellar, Spanish semejar.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sentar, from Vulgar Latin *sedentare, from Latin sedeō + *-entāre.

parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin sirpicularia.

From Old Galician-Portuguese singelo, from Vulgar Latin *singellus, from Latin singulus. Compare Spanish sencillo.

parole.significato: sovereign (exercising power to reign); regal, royal
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese, from a Vulgar Latin root *superānus, from Latin super. Compare French souverain, Italian sovrano, soprano, Spanish soberano. Doublet of soprano, from Italian.
From Old Galician-Portuguese sobro (from Vulgar Latin *sūberum, from Latin sūber) + -eiro, or directly from a Vulgar Latin *sūberārium.

From Old Galician-Portuguese solto, from Vulgar Latin *soltus, from Latin solutus.

parole.significato: serum (blood plasma from which the clotting proteins have been removed)

From Old Galician-Portuguese sessegar, from Vulgar Latin *sessicāre, from Latin sessus, past participle of sedeō.
From Vulgar Latin *sucāre, from Latin sūgere, from Proto-Indo-European *sug-, *suk-. Cognate with Galician sugar.

parole.significato: surge; outbreak (sudden rush or increase of something)

parole.significato: southern cattail (Typha domingensis, a reed native to tropical and temperate regions worldwide)

parole.significato: porpoise (any of the small cetacean species of the family Phocoenidae)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *thunnīna, from Latin thunnus (“tunna”). Cognate with Spanish toñina, Italian tonnina, Catalan tonyina.

parole.significato: to twist (to turn the ends in opposite directions)

parole.significato: to shear (to remove the fleece from a sheep)

parole.significato: to toast (to lightly cook by browning over fire)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin tostāre, from tostus, past participle of torreō.

parole.significato: to work (to do a specific task)

From a derivative of Old Galician-Portuguese trager (whence modern Portuguese trazer), from Vulgar Latin tragēre, from Latin trahō. Compare Galician traxe.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vagātīvus, from Latin vagor (“to wander”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *viridizāre. Derivable from verde (“green”) + -ejar (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: verdict (decision on an issue of fact in a civil or criminal case or an inquest)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin veredictum, from vere (“truly”) + dictum (“said”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese vermen, vermẽe, from Proto-Romance *verminem, from Latin vermis.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese vermelho (“red”), from Vulgar Latin *vermiclus, from Latin vermiculus (“little worm”), from vermis (“worm”), ultimately in reference to a scale insect of species Kermes vermilio, used to make a crimson dye. From Old Galician-Portuguese verão (“spring”), from Vulgar Latin *veranum (tempus), from Latin vēr (“spring”), from earlier *veror, from Proto-Italic *wezor, from Proto-Indo-European *wósr̥ (“spring”). Compare Galician verán, Spanish verano and Romanian vară.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *versicus, itself from Latin versus. Cognate with Spanish bizco and Asturian viesgu.

parole.significato: Striped wool cloth used for making clothes.
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from Vulgar Latin *venatum.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese vista, from Vulgar Latin *visita, from Latin visa, feminine past participle of videō.

parole.significato: visa (permit to enter and leave a country)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese visto, from Vulgar Latin *visitus, from Latin vīsus, perfect participle of videō (“to see”).

parole.significato: widow (a woman whose husband has died)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese viuva, from Vulgar Latin *viduva, from Classical Latin vidua (“widow”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁widʰéwh₂. Displaced Old Portuguese collateral form viuda, from the same Classical Latin word.

parole.significato: widowed (said of a person who is in a state of widowhood)
parole.testo: From Latin viduus, through a Vulgar Latin *viduvus.
From Old Galician-Portuguese volta (“turnaround”), from voltar (“to turn around”), from Vulgar Latin *vol(vi)tāre, derived from Latin volvere.
From Old Galician-Portuguese voltar, from Vulgar Latin *vol(vi)tāre, derived from Latin volvere.

parole.significato: a wild horse or a wild ass (Equus hydruntinus, an extinct equine)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese zebro, zevro (“wild ass”), from earlier ezebro, from Vulgar Latin *eciferus, from Latin equiferus (“wild horse”), from equus (“horse”) + ferus (“wild”).

parole.significato: juniper (shrub or tree of the genus Juniperus)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese, from an earlier form *jĩbro < *jĩebro, from Vulgar Latin ziniperus, from Latin iūniperus. Compare Galician cimbro, Spanish enebro. Doublet of the learned borrowing junípero.

Unknown. Possibly from: * Vulgar Latin *amidum, from Latin amylum (“starch”); * Arabic خَمَّجَ (ḵammaja, “to rot”); * Arabic اَلمُخّ (al-muḵḵ, “the marrow”). Cognate with Spanish hámago, Galician ámago and Catalan àmec.

parole.significato: strawberry tree (Arbutus unedo, a small, fruit-bearing tree of Europe)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *erbitus, from Latin arbutus (“strawberry tree”).
From água + -ar. Less likely from a Vulgar Latin *aquāre for Latin aquārī, or from adaquāre.
From a- + longo + -ar, or from Vulgar Latin *allongāre, from Late Latin elongāre, from Latin longus.

parole.significato: to threaten (to make a threat against someone; to use threats)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese amẽaçar, a variant of mẽaçar, either from mẽaça (“threat”) + -ar, or from a hypothetical Vulgar Latin *admināciāre (“to threaten”) < *mināciāre (“threaten”), from minācia (“threat”), from Latin mināciae. Cognate with English menace. Compare Catalan and Occitan amenaçar,
From a- + morto (“dead”) + -ecer, or from a Vulgar Latin *admortīre, *admortēscere, from Latin mortuus.

From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Vulgar Latin *appariclāre, *appariculāre, itself probably from Latin apparāre. Compare Spanish aparejar, French appareiller, Italian apparecchiare. Alternatively, it may be linked to Portuguese parelho, parelha.

parole.significato: to bet (to make a guess about the outcome of an event)
parole.testo: From aposta (“bet”) + -ar or from Vulgar Latin *appositāre, from Latin appositus.
From Old Galician-Portuguese aquen, from Vulgar Latin *eccum hinc, from Latin eccum + hinc, or from Vulgar Latin *eccum inde. Compare Spanish aquende, Italian quindi.

parole.significato: to monopolize; to take something for oneself without others benefiting of it
parole.testo: Uncertain, either: * From Old Galician-Portuguese *sobarcar, from Vulgar Latin *subbracchicāre, a compound of sub- + bracchium, cognate with Spanish sobarcar. * Inherited from Vulgar Latin ad se *imbracāre (“to tighten to oneself like trousers to a leg”), from a compound of in- + brāca.

parole.significato: paunch, fack, rumen (the first compartment of the stomach of ruminants)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from Latin ventriculus, diminutive of venter; or from Vulgar Latin *pantuclus, diminutive of pantex. Cognate with Galician bandullo, Asturian bandullu, banduyu, Spanish bandujo.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly inherited from a Vulgar Latin *opacius, variant of opacus (“darkened, opaque”), or from Latin badius (“reddish-brown”), both terms of uncertain origin.
Unknown. Perhaps related to Galician braña or from Vulgar Latin *vērānata, from Vulgar Latin *vērānum, via *verãada (compare dialectal gando). Compare also Galician branda.

parole.significato: rail (the metal bar that makes the track for a railroad)
parole.testo: From carro + -il, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *carrīlis, as an alteration of Late Latin currīlis, from Latin currus, with influence from carrus.

parole.significato: fence (thin barrier that separates two pieces of land)
parole.testo: Deverbal from cercar (“surround”), or from Old Galician-Portuguese cerca (“surround”), from a Vulgar Latin *circa (compare Spanish cerca, northern Italian cerca, French cerce), from the feminine of Latin circus.

From Old Galician-Portuguese cova, from Vulgar Latin *cova, from covus, alternative form of Latin cavus (or from a variant of Late Latin cava, from cavum, cavus), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱówHwos (“cavity”). Compare Spanish cueva.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; or from
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese dado, itself from a Vulgar Latin *dadu, of uncertain origin; possibly from Classical Arabic أَعْدَاد (ʔaʕdād, “numbers”), or from Latin datum. Compare Spanish dado, Catalan dau, Italian dado, French dé.
From Old Galician-Portuguese derramar, in turn from ramo, or from a Vulgar Latin *dīrāmāre or *dērāmāre, from Latin rāmus (“branch”). Compare Italian diramare, Romanian dărâma.

From Old Galician-Portuguese derrobar, from Vulgar Latin *dērūpāre, from Latin rūpēs (“cliff”). Alternatively from derribar, from de- + riba + -ar, from Latin rīpa. Compare Galician derrubar, cf. also Italian dirupare.

From Old Galician-Portuguese descalço, from Vulgar Latin *discalceus, itself either from a shortening of discalceātus, from Late Latin discalceō, or from Latin dis- + calceus. From gola, or from an Old Galician-Portuguese engolir, from a Vulgar Latin *ingullīre, from Latin gula.

parole.significato: to evil-eye (to cast an evil eye)

From en- + teso + -ar; or from Vulgar Latin *intēnsāre, from Latin intēnsus, whence Portuguese intenso. Compare Spanish entesar, Occitan entesar, Old French entaisier. See also teso.

parole.significato: to rub (move one object while maintaining contact with another object over some area)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exfricāre, from Latin ex- + fricō (“to rub”), or from an alteration of effricāre.

From falha, itself from a Vulgar Latin falla or falia (possibly partly through the intermediate or influence of Old French faille or Old Occitan), or from Old Galician-Portuguese fallar, from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin fallāre, from Latin fallere.

parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese faisca, feisca (attested in Medieval Latin as falisca), of uncertain origin. parole.significato: snout (long, projecting nose, mouth, and jaw of a beast)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin faucinus, a diminutive of Latin faucēs (“throat, gullet”). Alternatively, influenced by Spanish hocicar (“to root with the nose”), ultimately from Latin fodere (“to dig”). Cognate with Galician fociño. Compare also Spanish hocico and Asturian focicu.
Borrowed from French fraise or from Vulgar Latin *frēsāre, from frēsum, past participle of Latin frendēre (“to grind”). See also Spanish fresa.
From Old Galician-Portuguese grito, from gritar, from Vulgar Latin *crītāre, either from Latin quirītō or Frankish *krītan.
From Old Galician-Portuguese gru m, from Latin gruem f or m (“crane”) or possibly through a Vulgar Latin *gruum m, from Proto-Indo-European *gr̥h₂ú-, from *gerh₂- (“to cry hoarsely”).

parole.significato: a vat in which olives and grapes are pressed
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from lago or from a Vulgar Latin *lacālis, from Latin lacus.
From lavar + -dura, or from a Vulgar Latin root *lavatūra, from Latin lavō.

parole.significato: mottled (coloured in patches), spotted, speckled, piebald
parole.testo: From malha, or from Old Galician-Portuguese mallado, from an Iberian Vulgar Latin *mac(u)lātus, from Latin macula. Compare Spanish majada. From earlier mangal, from mango (“flail shaft”), from Vulgar Latin *manicus (“handle”), from Latin manus (“hand”). Alternatively, from Latin manuālis.

From piolho + -oso, or from Vulgar Latin peduclōsus, from Latin peduculōsus, variant of pēdīculōsus analogous to peduculus.
Uncertain. Either from Vulgar Latin *planea, from Latin plāna; from plana, feminine of plano; or a back-formation from aplainar.

From solto + -ar or alternatively from Vulgar Latin *soltāre (a root) < *solutāre, as a frequentative of Latin solvere.

Borrowed from Spanish zozobrar or Old Spanish sozobrar, from Old Catalan sotsobrar, from sotsobre < sots + sobre, or from a Vulgar Latin *subsuperāre (“turn upside down”), from sub (“under”) + super (“over”).

parole.significato: to emerge from the earth like a spring
parole.testo: From or related to surto, from Vulgar Latin *sūrctus, a corruption of Latin surrēctus, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *sūrctīre, derived from this root. Related to surgir. Alternatively from or influenced by Old French sourdre.
Either deverbal from tirotear or from Spanish tiroteo; otherwise directly from tiro. Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *tīrāre.

parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *tragāre, possibly from Doric Greek τράγω (trágō), in which case cognate with Attic Greek τρώγω (trṓgō, “to eat, to swallow”).
